# toolreader

Read-only viewer for what coding agents _did_ in T3 Code threads. It reads T3's SQLite database and shows each thread as a swimlane plus a turn → phase → action tree. Design notes live in `docs/spec.md`.

Setup, libraries and conventions are copied from `~/proj/t3code`. When in doubt, do what t3code does.

## The ways to hurt yourself

1. **Writing to the live T3 install.** `~/.t3/userdata` is the developer's real T3 database, in use while you work. toolreader opens it read-only, and it must stay that way. Never open it read-write, never run migrations against it, never "clean it up". For experiments, snapshot it (see Test data) and point `T3_DB` at the copy.
2. **Killing by pattern.** Never `pkill -f`, `pgrep | kill`, or kill a PID found by matching a name. Kill only a PID you captured at spawn, or the owner of your port from `lsof -nP -iTCP:<port> -sTCP:LISTEN` after confirming its cwd is this repo.
3. **Binding beyond localhost.** The server exposes every agent session on the machine. It binds `127.0.0.1`; keep it that way.

## Where code lives

- `src/core`: browser-safe code shared by server and web.
  - `domain.ts`: Schema domain models (Action, Message, ThreadView, …).
  - `api.ts`: the `HttpApi` contract. Server and client both derive from it; never put server code here.
  - `payload.ts`: Schemas for T3's raw activity payloads, for every provider.
  - `normalize.ts`, `shell.ts`, `tree.ts`: pure transforms, from raw rows to entries to tree.

## Verifying

- Run the smallest proof first: `vp test run <files>` for the tests you touched, then `vp check` (format and lint) and `vp run typecheck`.
- Changes to server behavior ship with focused tests. `ThreadStore` tests seed an in-memory SQLite database, and `Labeler` tests use a fake `codex` binary. Follow those patterns, and never call the real Codex from tests.
- Changes to normalization should also be run against the real data shape (a snapshot, as above), because providers emit payloads the unit tests don't cover.
- For UI changes, use the `test-toolreader` skill. Ask before opening browsers.

## Commits and PRs

- Conventional commit titles in plain language, e.g. `fix(viewer): failed searches no longer fold`.

I'm spotting the real quoting bug: Codex wraps commands like `/bin/zsh -lc 'cmd'`, escaping inner single quotes as `'"'"'`, but the trimMatchingOuterQuotes function naively strips just the first and last character, which mangles those escaped sequences and causes weird tokenization.

The right fix is to use the tokenizer to properly unquote the shell word after `-lc`, taking the single resulting word token if there's exactly one. Before implementing, I want to check real rollout data, existing tests, and the codex version/app-server format to confirm the pattern holds.

I'm realizing there's no direct link between the exec call_id and nested exec-* ids, since in code-mode exec scripts can call shell commands, MCP tools, or apply_patch internally. For dedup purposes, I should treat each exec custom call as a single action, special-casing the common pattern where the script is just a single exec_command call so it renders as that shell command directly, and falling back to something else otherwise.

Otherwise I'd show it as a generic "run js" action, but the problem is nested MCP calls inside the script would get shown twice — once as the exec wrapper, once as the nested tool call. My fix is structural: if any nested item completes between the exec call's start and output lines, that means the nested items already represent it, so I should skip synthesizing the wrapper and let the nested items speak for themselves; otherwise synthesize it normally. This also generalizes nicely to the `wait` call, which continues a code-mode cell and carries forward the script's output for long-running commands.

For `write_stdin`, I want to merge its output back into the originating `exec_command` by session ID — so "Process running with session ID 4051" followed later by "Process exited with code 0" collapses into one entry with the exit code attached, while empty-character polling gets dropped and only meaningful stdin writes show as a distinct action. This feels worth the complexity since it's exactly how long-running test sessions show up, so I want to keep it in scope but implemented simply. Now I want to quantify how common each of these patterns actually is before finalizing the conversion table.

For the per-tool mapping, I'm working out how to parse each call type into a display item: exec_command maps exit codes and "running with session" into commandExecution with the output text after "Output:\n"; shell takes the argv array and needs shell-quoted joining similar to Codex's own shlex-style display; shell_command parses its own exit code/wall time/output format; local_shell_call seems rare enough to skip; and apply_patch needs parsing of the patch header lines ("*** Update File:", "*** Add File:", "*** Delete File:", "*** Move to:") along with unified diff hunks to reconstruct file changes.

For apply_patch's `@@` markers, I realize these are often bare or just context headers without real line numbers, so my existing unified-diff detection regex would misfire and produce broken diffs. Since I can't know the real line numbers for synthesized patches, I'll fabricate hunk headers with line counts and mark them as non-exact (exactLines: false), and determine success/failure by checking whether the output text starts with "Success".

For MCP calls, I'm working out how to parse the namespace into server and tool fields, since older formats don't always have the "mcp__" prefix and the naming conventions vary (e.g. "context7__get-library-docs" vs "codex_apps__github").

For other function calls like web.run, clock.sleep, or custom exec calls, I'm planning to map them to a generic tool call with a title built from the name and arguments, treating web.run specifically as a search query.

For commandExecution, I need to extract the shell command via regex from the script content when it uses tools.exec_command, and construct output text starting with "Script completed" plus wall time and output.
